title: How Can I Reduce Crop Losses on My Farm?
metaTitle: Reduce Crop Losses: Field, Weather, Harvest and Storage
metaDescription: Reduce crop losses from pests, typhoons, late harvest and poor drying, with clear steps for palay and the records that show where your losses happen.
excerpt: To reduce crop losses, find where your farm loses the most and fix that first: pests caught late, storms met unprepared, a harvest cut too early or too late, and grain dried or stored badly. Every year pests take as much as 40 percent of the crops grown on Earth. For rice, a 2010 study put losses after harvest at 16.47 percent. The farm app anee.io, built for Filipino farmers, helps by dating each task to the crop's stage, flagging weather risks and keeping the records that show where the losses came from.

blocks.text:
Losses come in four places. In the field, pests, diseases, weeds and rats take part of the crop. Then the weather takes its share through typhoons, floods and drought. At harvest, a field cut too early or too late loses grain and quality. After that, poor drying and storage crack and spoil what was saved.

The same figures point to milling, where 5.52 percent is lost. It links those losses to broken or cracked grains, which often come from improper drying. So the fix for a milling loss may start on the drying floor, days earlier.

items: Find your biggest loss first. Records by lot and season show where it is.
In the field, monitor from the early stage and name the problem before you spray.
Track storms early, and bring in ripe fields before the wind arrives.
Harvest palay when 85 to 90 percent of the grains are golden, and thresh within a day in the wet season.
Dry within 12 to 24 hours to 12 to 14 percent moisture, and store the grain dry.

blocks.text: How do you reduce crop losses in the field?

Pest control starts with prevention. Use varieties resistant to the pests in your area, and rotate them every 2 to 4 croppings. Plant in step with your neighbors after a 30 day rest period. Then monitor the field regularly from the early stage, so you catch pests while they are few. Insecticide is a last resort, after cultural, biological and physical control.

Spare the natural enemies too. Spiders feed on planthoppers and leafhoppers, and careless spraying upsets that balance. When you see damage, name the cause before you buy anything. Our guides on [pest or disease](/blog/pest-or-disease-how-to-tell) and [early pest detection](/blog/early-pest-detection) help. The [pest and disease finders](/features/pest-and-disease-finders) also work from your crop and the damage you see.
How do you cut losses from typhoons and floods?

Time is the main tool. Wind Signal Number 1 gives 36 hours of lead time, and Signals 4 and 5 give only 12 hours. Already at Signal 2, rice at flowering or ripening can take considerable damage. So follow each storm from the first bulletin, and agree in advance when you will harvest, drain or secure the grain. Our guide on how to [track typhoons](/blog/track-typhoons-near-my-farm) shows how.

Insurance covers what you cannot save. With PCIC rice crop insurance, a notice of loss may go first by text or email. The written claim follows. Ask your PCIC office which risks your policy covers. Dated photos and the crop's stage help the claim. Our guide to [farm records for loans](/blog/farm-records-for-loans-and-insurance) lists what to keep.
How do you cut losses at harvest and after?

items.title: Drain before harvest
items.text: Drain the field 1 to 2 weeks before the expected harvest, so the crop ripens evenly and the grain stays dry.

items.title: Harvest at the right maturity
items.text: Cut when 85 to 90 percent of the grains have turned golden, or 90 to 95 percent for a combine. With a moisture meter, expect 20 to 25 percent in the wet season and 18 to 21 in the dry.

items.title: Thresh on time
items.text: Thresh within one day in the wet season or two in the dry. Avoid threshing dripping wet palay in a machine, and keep most engine threshers near 800 rpm.

items.title: Dry within 12 to 24 hours
items.text: In a mechanical dryer, keep the air no hotter than 50 to 70 degrees C, for 5 to 8 hours. In the sun, use clean concrete, stir at least every 30 minutes and keep the rain off.

items.title: Store clean and dry
items.text: Store grain at 12 to 14 percent moisture. Leave air spaces in each pile, keep piles to 6 or 7 bags, and keep one meter from walls and roof frames.

blocks.title: Do not leave cut palay piled for more than a day
blocks.text: Piles of cut palay heat up and discolor the grain, which lowers the quality of the milled rice. So plan the thresher before you plan the reapers, especially in the wet season.
How does anee.io help reduce crop losses?

Losses shrink when work happens on time. In anee.io, every task carries a date from its lot's own day zero. The [growth stages](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) page gives each lot a watch list for its stage. The forecast sits beside the plan, with a reminder when rain falls on a spray day. For storms, Satellite Weather shows each typhoon's path and its distance from your field.

After harvest, [observations](/features/harvest-records) record each lot's yield, moisture, price, buyer and the problems you saw. Then Anee, the smart farm technician, can write a season report on what went well and what went wrong. Compare Reports holds two seasons side by side. Those records point to the stage that leaks the most, so next season you fix that one first.

items.q: What causes the most crop loss on Filipino farms?
items.a: It differs by farm and by season. Pests, typhoons and losses after harvest are the big three. Pests take up to 40 percent of crop production worldwide. A 2010 study put rice losses after harvest at 16.47 percent. Your own records show which one hits your farm hardest.

items.q: How much palay is lost after harvest?
items.a: A 2010 study found 16.47 percent lost after harvest. Milling alone accounted for 5.52 percent, often from grains cracked by improper drying.

items.q: When is palay ready to harvest?
items.a: Harvest when 85 to 90 percent of the grains have turned golden yellow, or 90 to 95 percent for a combine. Grain moisture then runs about 20 to 25 percent in the wet season and 18 to 21 in the dry.

items.q: How fast should I dry palay after threshing?
items.a: Within 12 to 24 hours, down to 12 to 14 percent moisture. Cut palay left in piles heats up and loses quality.

items.q: Can crop insurance cover my losses?
items.a: PCIC offers rice crop insurance. A notice of loss can go first by text or email. Ask your PCIC office which risks your policy covers and the current deadlines.
